intro: Read the deck for the ideas and these notes for the thinking. Each note says what a slide is for, how to hold it in memory and where practitioners slip. Work the examples in pencil, test yourself with the recall questions, and apply each tool to a behaviour you actually work on.

sections.title: What BCC & SBCC Are
sections.big_idea: BCC is communication built around one behaviour, one audience and its barriers. **SBCC adds the social and service conditions** the message assumes.
in_plain_words: Behaviour Change Communication is the planned use of communication to move people from intention to action. It sits apart from advertising and from health education alone. Every behaviour rests on a chain of preconditions (soap and water, a working toilet, a held immunisation session), and most are not communication problems. Name the whole chain before you design a message.

Early programmes focused on the individual. The field added an S, for Social and Behaviour Change Communication, when practitioners learned that families, norms, services and policy also shape behaviour. Most campaigns stop at awareness, and the real work lies in the drop-offs between awareness, knowledge, intention, action and maintenance. **Communication is one lever among several**, and it cannot supply soap, toilets, vaccines or clinics.

diagram.caption: the behaviour chain, with a leak at every step

key_terms.meaning: Planned communication that promotes and sustains behaviour change.
Social and Behaviour Change Communication: works across individual, community and norm levels.
A condition that must be true for a behaviour, such as a working toilet.
High awareness with low practice, the pattern of a weak campaign.
Keeping up the behaviour every time, after starting.

worked_example.title: Find where the funnel leaks
worked_example.setup: An illustrative district surveys 1,000 mothers about ORS: 900 are aware, 600 have knowledge, 400 intend to use it, 200 gave it in the last episode.
steps: Intention to action: 200 ÷ 400 = 50% of intenders did not act.
Share of the aware who acted: 200 ÷ 900 = 22.2%.
worked_example.answer: The sharpest relative drop is intention to action, at 50%, so friction, cues and cost need attention before more awareness work.

mistakes: Measuring recall and calling the campaign a success while practice has not moved.
Using more posters as a stand-in for change, because output is countable.
Calling people ignorant, which ends the search for the real barrier.
Claiming the broader SBCC frame while designing for one individual receiving one message.

recall.q: What does the S in SBCC add?
recall.a: Attention to families, norms, services and policy, in addition to the individual.

recall.q: Name the five steps of the behaviour chain.
recall.a: Awareness, knowledge, intention, action and maintenance.

recall.q: Give two things SBCC cannot do alone.
recall.a: Any two of: supply soap, toilets, vaccines or clinics; fix a hostile or distant service; remove the cost of changing.

recall.q: What is the signature pattern of a weak campaign?
recall.a: High awareness with low practice.

recall.q: What should you do before designing a message?
recall.a: Name the whole chain of preconditions for the behaviour.

sections.title: Why Behaviour Is Hard to Change
sections.big_idea: Knowledge is necessary and almost never sufficient. **Name the gap, find the real barrier**, and make the behaviour easy before you make it desired.
in_plain_words: The oldest assumption in health communication is that people who knew better would do better. Smoking is the standard counter-example: awareness of harm is near-universal. There are two gaps. Information closes the knowledge gap, while cues, skills and removing friction close the intention-action gap, which is harder and more neglected. Intentions fail through forgetting, friction, habit, present bias and competing demands.

Behaviour is also watched and judged. The person acting is often not the person deciding, and structural barriers such as a missing toilet, an absent nurse or a lost day's wage are outside the individual's control. When a behaviour is hard even strong motivation fails, so **reduce friction first and then motivate**. Formative research finds the real barrier before the campaign is designed.

diagram.caption: four families of barrier, four kinds of response

key_terms.meaning: The belief that giving people facts will change what they do.
Planning to act and not doing so.
Valuing now over later, so costs today outweigh later benefits.
A family member or elder who decides whether the behaviour happens.
An obstacle outside the individual's control that no message can move.
Any inconvenience that makes the behaviour harder.

worked_example.title: Which gap is larger?
worked_example.setup: An illustrative survey finds that 80% know how to use a toilet properly, 60% intend to, and 30% do.
steps: The larger gap is intention to practice, so the response is cues, defaults and reduced friction, plus a check for structural barriers.
worked_example.answer: The intention-action gap (30 points) is larger than the knowledge gap (20 points), so more information is the wrong first move.

mistakes: Treating a structural barrier as an attitude problem and running a campaign against a wall.
Pouring budget into motivation because communication budgets can buy it.
Treating antenatal visits, vasectomy or menstrual hygiene as private decisions.
Cutting formative research, though a week of it costs less than aiming at the wrong barrier.

recall.q: What closes the knowledge gap, and what closes the intention-action gap?
recall.a: Information and demonstration close the first; cues, defaults and reduced friction close the second.

recall.q: Name three reasons intentions fail.
recall.a: Any three of: forgetting, friction, habit, present bias, competing demands.

recall.q: What is the most reliable fix for habit?
recall.a: Attach the new act to an existing routine.

recall.q: Who are the gatekeepers for an antenatal visit?
recall.a: The mother-in-law and neighbours.

recall.q: What is the most expensive mistake in SBCC, per the deck?
recall.a: Diagnosing a structural barrier as an attitude problem.

sections.title: Individual Behaviour Theories
sections.big_idea: Theories are maps that tell you what to ask. **Formative research tells you what is true here**, and good programmes borrow constructs from several.
in_plain_words: The Health Belief Model says people act when they think a threat is real and acting is worth it: susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues to action and self-efficacy. Its gift to communicators is that perceived barriers often outweigh perceived benefits, so lowering the felt cost of acting beats raising fear. The Theory of Planned Behaviour builds intention from attitude, subjective norm and perceived control.

The Transtheoretical Model adds stages (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance) and warns against aiming one message at a mixed audience. Each stage has its own communication job and its own best channel. No single theory explains everything, so **say which construct your design targets**. COM-B, later in the course, is the most usable synthesis.

diagram.caption: what each theory tells you to ask

key_terms.meaning: Health Belief Model: action follows perceived threat and perceived worth of acting.
The felt cost of acting; often the deciding construct.
Theory of Planned Behaviour: attitude, norm and control build intention.
The felt sense of 'I can do this' that also affects action directly.
Prochaska and DiClemente's stages of change.
Grouping an audience by readiness so each gets a fitting message.

worked_example.title: How much of a mixed audience fits an 'act now' message?
worked_example.setup: An illustrative group of 200 women: 80 in precontemplation, 60 in contemplation, 40 in preparation and 20 in action or maintenance.
steps: Share a how-to message can serve: 60 ÷ 200 = 30%.
worked_example.answer: A single 'act now' message fits only 30% of this audience, so segment by stage and match the job to each.

mistakes: Designing straight from a theory, which addresses whichever construct it emphasises and skips the diagnosis.
Preaching attitude when the real block is felt control.
Giving a detailed how-to to someone in precontemplation, or more facts to someone in contemplation.
Assuming the answer will be about perception when it is about permission.

recall.q: Which HBM construct most often decides the outcome and is addressed least?
recall.a: Perceived barriers.

recall.q: What does TPB add over the Theory of Reasoned Action?
recall.a: Perceived behavioural control.

recall.q: Name the five stages of change.
recall.a: Precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance.

recall.q: What is the communication job in contemplation?
recall.a: Tip the balance and show benefits.

recall.q: Which question in the HBM table sits outside the model?
recall.a: Who decides whether she goes.

sections.title: Social & Environmental Theories
sections.big_idea: Behaviour sits in nested layers. **People copy credible, similar models**, and where norms govern, collective change removes the cost of being first.
in_plain_words: The socio-ecological model is a checklist of layers: person, family and peers, community, institutions and services, policy and society. Most campaigns work on the inner layers while the binding constraint sits in the outer ones. Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory says people learn by observing, especially similar others who are rewarded, and self-efficacy is built by mastery, modelling and trusted encouragement.

Rogers described how new practices spread in waves from a small group of early adopters, so coverage measured against the whole population from month one looks like failure. Social norms come in two kinds: descriptive (what people do) and injunctive (what they approve of). Saying that most people still do the bad thing makes it look normal. **Lead with a trend or an injunctive norm** when the descriptive norm is against you.

key_terms.meaning: A checklist of nested layers of influence on behaviour.
Belief in one's ability to perform a specific behaviour.
Copying behaviour seen in credible models.
Rogers: ideas spread in sequence, led by early adopters.
What I believe most people actually do.
What I believe most people approve of.

worked_example.title: Early coverage looks small
worked_example.setup: A village of 900 households starts a handwashing station programme. About a third are the early majority, who wait for proof from people like them. In month one, 45 households adopt.
steps: If all of them follow the early adopters: 45 + 300 = 345 households.
worked_example.answer: A 5% start is normal for diffusion, and the early adopters are the route to 38.3% once the early majority sees proof.

mistakes: Designing for the innermost layer only and ignoring family, community and service layers.
Using aspirational celebrities when a model similar in age, caste, income and setting works better.
Telling people that 'too many still' do the bad behaviour, which normalises it.
Judging coverage against the whole population from the first month.

recall.q: Who proposed Social Cognitive Theory?
recall.a: Albert Bandura.

recall.q: What raises self-efficacy most strongly?
recall.a: Mastery experience, doing it successfully once.

recall.q: What is the difference between descriptive and injunctive norms?
recall.a: Descriptive is what people do; injunctive is what they approve of.

recall.q: Why does collective change help in norm-governed behaviour?
recall.a: The first person to change bears a social cost, and collective change removes it.

recall.q: Who are the opinion leaders in diffusion?
recall.a: People who bridge to the majority; they are rarely the formally powerful.

sections.title: Behavioural Economics & Nudges
sections.big_idea: People use shortcuts in predictable ways, so **design the choice**. COM-B diagnoses what is missing, and nudges work only alongside real systems.
in_plain_words: Behavioural economics shows that people use mental shortcuts and are swayed by framing, in ways that are systematic and so can be designed for. COM-B says a behaviour needs capability, opportunity and motivation at once. Find the missing one and the intervention type follows. In development settings opportunity is missing most often, and communication addresses it least.

Biases become levers: present bias, loss aversion, status quo bias, social proof and availability. A nudge changes how choices are presented without forbidding options or changing incentives, as with defaults, framing, commitment, reminders and simplification. The design of the choice environment is never neutral. EAST (easy, attractive, social, timely) is a quick field test. **Nudges work at the margin** and cannot supply a missing service.

diagram.note: all three must hold at once; the missing one tells you what to fix

key_terms.meaning: Michie's model: capability, opportunity and motivation produce behaviour.
A change in presentation that steers behaviour without forbidding options.
The automatic option; changing it moves uptake.
Losing ₹100 hurts more than gaining ₹100 pleases.
How the decision environment is set up: defaults, order, friction, salience.
Easy, attractive, social, timely: a four-check field test.

worked_example.title: Diagnose with COM-B and simplify
worked_example.setup: At an illustrative clinic a mother knows how to sign up, wants to attend, but the sign-up takes four steps and the desk closes early. The team cuts the process to two steps.
steps: Capability is present (she knows how), and motivation is present (she wants to).
Opportunity is missing: the context blocks the behaviour.
worked_example.answer: Opportunity is the missing component, and simplification removes half the steps, which does more than another round of messaging.

mistakes: Running a motivation campaign to fix an opportunity problem.
Calling a large payment a nudge. A nudge leaves incentives roughly unchanged.
Using a nudge as a replacement for structural fixes, such as asking people to wash hands where there is no water.
Using concealed persuasion techniques you would not explain to the audience.

recall.q: What are the three COM-B components?
recall.a: Capability, opportunity and motivation.

recall.q: Which component is missing most often in development settings?
recall.a: Opportunity.

recall.q: Name two nudge types.
recall.a: Any two of: default, framing, commitment, reminder, simplification.

recall.q: What does EAST stand for?
recall.a: Easy, attractive, social, timely.

recall.q: What is the transparency test for nudges?
recall.a: Would you be comfortable telling the audience exactly what you did and why?

sections.title: Knowing Your Audience
sections.big_idea: There is no such thing as 'the public'. **Segment by barrier**, reach the secondary audience and gatekeepers, and write one human insight.
in_plain_words: A village contains many audiences: a new mother, her mother-in-law, the ASHA, the village head, an absent husband. Speaking to everyone usually means reaching no one. Segmentation by barrier changes the design more than demographic cuts, because two women of the same age and income may face different obstacles. Layer your audiences as primary, secondary and influencing.

Budgets usually go all to the primary audience while the decision often sits with the secondary one, and in much of South Asia the gatekeeper is the real audience. Find barriers and motivators in research and pair them. A persona makes the segment a named, concrete person, built from real interviews. The goal is one sharp insight in the person's own emotional logic. **A good insight suggests a message you would not have written otherwise.**

diagram.caption: three audience layers for antenatal care, outermost first

key_terms.meaning: Dividing a population into groups sharing barriers or motivations.
The person whose behaviour must change.
Those close to her who shape the behaviour.
The mother-in-law, husband or elder who holds the decision.
A named, concrete character built from real interviews.
The true, often surprising reason a person acts or does not.

worked_example.title: Reallocate a budget toward the secondary audience
worked_example.setup: An illustrative campaign budget of ₹10 lakh goes entirely to the pregnant woman. The team moves 30% to the mother-in-law and husband, the secondary audience.
steps: Amount left for the primary audience: 10 − 3 = 7 lakh.
Design at least one message and one channel for the secondary audience.
worked_example.answer: ₹3 lakh to the secondary audience and ₹7 lakh to the primary, a reallocation the deck calls the highest-return available in most campaigns.

mistakes: Writing one message for 'the community', which is too general to move anyone.
Segmenting by demographics only, which tells you who they are and not why they are not acting.
Treating gatekeepers as obstacles when they are an audience with their own motivators.
Building a persona in a workshop from imagination.

recall.q: Name the three audience layers.
recall.a: Primary, secondary and influencing (tertiary).

recall.q: Which segmentation cut does the deck call the most useful?
recall.a: By barrier faced.

recall.q: What would move a mother-in-law?
recall.a: Status, a healthy grandchild and her own experience honoured.

recall.q: Which barrier do motivators rarely outweigh, per slide 51?
recall.a: Lost wages; the answer there is compensation or timing.

recall.q: What is the test of a good insight?
recall.a: It suggests a message you would not have written otherwise.

sections.title: Formative Research
sections.big_idea: Listen before you design. **Compare doers with non-doers**, probe levers as well as facts, and size the problem with existing data.
in_plain_words: Formative research is early, exploratory listening that shapes the intervention before messages, materials or channels are fixed. It answers what people do, why, what would move them, whom they trust and which words they use. It need not be large: twenty in-depth interviews and two days of observation answer most for one behaviour in one district. It is skipped because it sits between funding and visible output.

Choose methods by purpose: interviews for sensitive behaviour, focus groups for norms and language, observation for the say-do gap, free listing for local categories and a quick survey for how common. Barrier analysis picks one specific behaviour, interviews doers and non-doers and ranks the differences in belief. **The biggest gap is your priority barrier.** Qualitative work comes first, then a quick scan sizes the problem, and research continues into pretesting.

key_terms.meaning: Early research that shapes an intervention before design.
A structured comparison of practisers and non-practisers.
People who do the behaviour and people who do not.
The difference between what people report and what they do.
A detailed one-to-one interview, good for sensitive topics.
Showing drafts to the real audience before mass production.

worked_example.title: Find the barrier that separates doers from non-doers
worked_example.setup: An illustrative barrier analysis interviews 45 doers and 45 non-doers about attending antenatal care. 38 doers and 14 non-doers say the mother-in-law approves. 20 doers and 27 non-doers say the cost is a problem.
worked_example.answer: The approval gap (53.3 points) is far larger than the cost gap (15.6), so design first for the mother-in-law's approval.

mistakes: Skipping formative research because it delays visible output.
Asking 'do you know X?' and taking reported knowledge as a predictor of practice.
Using focus groups to estimate how common a behaviour is.
Running a survey before the qualitative work, with questions in the wrong words.

recall.q: What is the commonest cause of campaign failure, per the deck?
recall.a: Skipping formative research.

recall.q: Which method best shows the say-do gap?
recall.a: Observation.

recall.q: What do the barrier analysis steps start with?
recall.a: Picking one specific behaviour.

recall.q: Why ask about the last actual instance?
recall.a: Recall of a specific episode is far more accurate than a self-description.

recall.q: What data should you use before commissioning a survey?
recall.a: Existing sources such as NFHS, HMIS and district reports.

sections.title: Designing Messages
sections.big_idea: One audience, one behaviour, one ask. **Pretest before you print**, and end with a what, where and when.
in_plain_words: The Single Overriding Communication Objective names one audience, one behaviour, one change and one reason. If it takes more than one sentence, the campaign is trying to do more than one thing. Putting several behaviours on one poster leaves the audience remembering the logo. Effective messages use emotion to open and reason to close, with the action stated plainly at the end.

Fear works only when paired with a doable action and fails when the threat feels remote or people feel helpless. A memorable message is simple, concrete, credible, emotional and story-shaped. The messenger matters: a relatable neighbour for everyday behaviours, an elder for permission, a celebrity for attention. Pretest comprehension, attractiveness, acceptability, persuasion and self-reference with eight to twelve people. **A call to action needs what, where and when.**

right.title: Doable ask
items: Take your baby for the 9-month measles shot
Wash with soap before feeding your child
Go to the sub-centre on Tuesday morning
Use the toilet at the end of your lane

key_terms.meaning: Single Overriding Communication Objective: one change for one audience.
Facts, benefits and evidence.
Feeling, identity and story.
A threat message; works only with a doable action.
The source of the message; credibility is part of the message.
The team cannot see that an image or metaphor is unclear to others.

worked_example.title: Read a pretest and count the cost
worked_example.setup: An illustrative pretest shows a poster to 10 members of the real audience. 6 misread the main image. The planned print run is 50,000 posters at ₹8 each.
worked_example.answer: 60% misread the image, so redraw it before spending the ₹4 lakh print run.

mistakes: Cramming nutrition, hygiene, immunisation and family planning onto one poster.
Presenting a threat without an immediately available action.
Choosing a celebrity for persuasion when a relatable neighbour does better for everyday behaviours.
Leaving out the where and when of the ask.

recall.q: What four things does a SOCO name?
recall.a: One audience, one behaviour, one change and one reason.

recall.q: When does fear work?
recall.a: When paired with a doable action, personal threat, high self-efficacy and sparing use.

recall.q: Which five qualities make a message memorable?
recall.a: Simple, concrete, credible, emotional and story-shaped.

recall.q: What is the best messenger for a behaviour needing permission?
recall.a: A respected elder.

recall.q: How many people does the deck suggest for pretesting?
recall.a: Eight to twelve members of the real audience.

sections.title: Channels & the Communication Mix
sections.big_idea: Reach and depth trade off, so every serious campaign is a mix. **Layer one consistent message** and sequence: broadcast to seed, contact to convert.
in_plain_words: Mass media reaches millions and persuades shallowly, mid-media and folk forms bring local credibility, interpersonal contact persuades and answers doubts, and digital channels are timely and two-way. No family does both reach and depth, and cost per person moves the opposite way to persuasion. Community mobilisation turns private intention into a collective commitment that holds after the campaign ends.

Each channel has a weakness to plan for: mass media cannot answer a family's doubt, folk forms vary by troupe and night, interpersonal contact depends on a worker's time, and phone access skews male, richer, younger and urban. The reminder is the highest-value digital use. Match channels to audience, job, stage and moment, and **layer them so the same message repeats**. Sequence deliberately and budget realistically.

key_terms.meaning: The combination of channels, each doing what it does best.
Street plays, puppets, folk song, video vans, wall painting.
Interpersonal communication: counselling, peer groups and home visits.
Organising groups to hold the behaviour as shared commitment.
Interactive voice response, which reaches non-readers by phone.
Repeating one consistent message across channels.

worked_example.title: What does home counselling cost in time?
worked_example.setup: An illustrative block plans one 20-minute home counselling visit to each of 5,000 households, shared among 6 ASHAs.
steps: Say what the 278 hours displace, because the ASHA's day is already full.
worked_example.answer: About 278 hours of extra work per ASHA, which the programme must offset with time, pay or dropped tasks.

mistakes: Relying on one channel and choosing which half of the job to leave undone.
Planning media from urban assumptions and underestimating radio in rural South Asia.
Assuming a live performance carries the same message every night.
Texting a household phone about a woman's health without checking who reads it.

recall.q: Which channel family gives reach and norm-setting?
recall.a: Mass media.

recall.q: What is the highest-value digital use?
recall.a: The reminder, which addresses the intention-action gap at the decision moment.

recall.q: Why is interpersonal contact limited?
recall.a: It is the most expensive per person and depends on the worker's time.

recall.q: What sequence does the deck advise?
recall.a: Mass media first, interpersonal contact after, reminders at the decision point.

recall.q: Which platform is usually cheapest for community mobilisation?
recall.a: An existing SHG network.

sections.title: Campaigns & Community Engagement
sections.big_idea: A campaign is a loop built on a written strategy. **Ownership sustains change**, so build community-led approaches and budget the maintenance phase.
in_plain_words: The SBCC cycle runs analyse, design, develop and pretest, implement, monitor and evaluate, then back to analysis. Behind it sits a written strategy: behaviour, audiences, barriers, SOCO, channels, messengers and indicators, all before creative work. The logo and tagline come last. A slogan with no strategy behind it is the standard failure.

When a community diagnoses its own problem the change holds. CLTS triggers a whole-community decision and works through norm change, with a stigma risk for the poorest. Entertainment-education draws on Bandura and needs a good story. Frontline workers carry interpersonal SBCC and are the most over-subscribed resource. Participatory women's groups have strong evidence for maternal and newborn outcomes. **Remove friction so the easy choice is the healthy one.**

key_terms.meaning: Behaviour, audiences, barriers, SOCO, channels, messengers and indicators.
Community-Led Total Sanitation, pioneered by Kamal Kar in Bangladesh.
A facilitated process that leads a community to decide to act.
Open-defecation-free community.
Behaviour messages woven into stories audiences love.
A group that discusses problems, plans and supports change.

worked_example.title: Budget the maintenance phase
worked_example.setup: An illustrative SBCC plan has ₹50 lakh over 12 months. Most funding covers the launch and stops when reinforcement matters most, so the team sets aside 20% for reinforcement and a mid-course review.
steps: Mid-course review point in a 12-month plan: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 months.
Give the review explicit licence to change the creative.
worked_example.answer: ₹10 lakh reserved for reinforcement, ₹40 lakh for launch, with a review at month 6.

mistakes: Starting from a slogan and reverse-engineering a strategy.
Treating the cycle as a line, so no mechanism exists to discover that the message is misread.
Using CLTS-style triggering in a way that shames households that lack the means to build.
Routing new communication tasks through ASHAs without saying what they displace.

recall.q: Name the five stages of the SBCC cycle.
recall.a: Analyse, design, develop and pretest, implement, monitor and evaluate.

recall.q: Who pioneered CLTS?
recall.a: Kamal Kar, in Bangladesh.

recall.q: What is the main critique of CLTS?
recall.a: Triggering can shame the poorest households, who often lack the means but have the will.

recall.q: Which theory sits behind entertainment-education?
recall.a: Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory.

recall.q: Which of the five sustaining moves is most durable?
recall.a: Removing friction, since ease does not decay like motivation.

sections.title: Monitoring, Ethics & Examples
sections.big_idea: Follow the chain from outputs to behaviour. **Persuasion must respect people**, and the Indian examples show the lessons at work.
in_plain_words: Monitoring must follow the chain: outputs, reach, exposure, knowledge and attitude, behaviour, impact. Programmes routinely report the first two and claim the last. Pair each level with an indicator, including a norm indicator, and verify behaviour against records where possible, since self-reported handwashing is higher than observed.

Four Indian examples carry the lessons. Handwashing moved from germs to moments. Mission Indradhanush paired service drives with rumour response. Swachh Bharat showed the gap between construction and use. ORS shows one behaviour promoted consistently for decades. The ethics rules are no stigma, truthfulness, respect for autonomy, do no harm and inclusion. **Four traps** (stigma, norm, fear, blame) are avoidable at the drafting stage.

diagram.caption: the monitoring chain, with an indicator at each level

key_terms.meaning: What you produced: posters printed, spots aired.
People who did see or hear the message.
The share who believe neighbours approve; often omitted.
India's drive combining service delivery with communication on immunisation.
Shaming people who lack the means but not the will.
Saying most people still do the bad behaviour, which normalises it.

worked_example.title: Read an indicator chain
worked_example.setup: An illustrative immunisation campaign targets 10,000 mothers. 6,000 recall the message, 4,500 can state when to immunise, and 1,500 have fully immunised children.
steps: Gap between knowledge and behaviour: 45 − 15 = 30 points.
worked_example.answer: Exposure is 60% and behaviour only 15%, so the failure sits between knowledge and action, a precise and useful result.

mistakes: Reporting posters printed or spots aired as results.
Accepting self-reported handwashing as the observed rate.
Urging a woman to act against her household's wishes without asking what follows for her.
Counting toilets built as the behaviour change, when use is the real measure.

recall.q: What does reach prove, and what does behaviour prove?
recall.a: Reach proves people could have seen it; behaviour proves it worked.

recall.q: Which indicator is most often omitted and most diagnostic for norm-governed behaviour?
recall.a: The norm indicator, a single survey question.

recall.q: What was the key lesson of Mission Indradhanush?
recall.a: Communication and service must move together; rumour response matters most.

recall.q: What is the gap that Swachh Bharat exposed?
recall.a: Between construction of toilets and their sustained use.

recall.q: Name the four traps in the avoiding-harm slide.
recall.a: Stigma, norm, fear and blame.

notes.2: Eleven sections run from definitions through theory, audience, research, messages, channels and campaigns to monitoring and ethics. Sections 2 to 5 give the diagnosis tools and sections 6 to 9 the design tools. **Skim the agenda, then read in order**, since later sections keep returning to the barrier idea.
notes.4: BCC is communication designed around a specific behaviour, audience and barrier, which separates it from advertising and from health education alone. The table lists what must be true for each behaviour, and most items are not communication problems. **Name the whole chain before designing a message**, then pick the links communication can fix.
notes.5: The added S is the shift from persuading one person to working across individual, community and social-norm levels, and also with services and policy. Use the two-column table as a self-check: if your programme designs for one individual receiving one message, **it is doing BCC and should say so**.
notes.6: Read the five steps as a ladder with a leak at each rung. The table names what stops each rung: a vague message, no benefit or hostile norms, friction and cost, no cue. Campaigns are designed for the first step and evaluated at the fourth. **Diagnose which step your audience is stuck at** before writing anything.
notes.7: High awareness with low practice is the signature of a weak campaign, and a campaign built for reach will produce it. The chart is illustrative, so read its shape. **Make the gap your target** and treat awareness as secondary, because measuring recall alone shows success while behaviour stays put.
notes.8: Four misconceptions, each kept alive because it suits reporting: more posters (output is countable), one-off campaigns (they fit a project cycle), 'people are ignorant' (it requires nothing of the programme), mass media is enough (it is visible to funders). **Resist the blame framing in team discussions**, because it ends the search for the real barrier.
notes.9: SBCC is one lever. The left list says what it can do (attitudes, skills, cues) and the right list what it cannot (supply, services, cost). Where you find a structural block, **flag it to whoever can fix it** and avoid communicating harder around it. Use the table to spot missing supply, delivery or quality.
notes.10: The roadmap divides the course into understanding (why behaviour resists, theories, behavioural economics) and designing and delivering (audience, research, messages, channels, campaigns, monitoring and ethics). All examples come from India and the region. **Use it as a checklist for your own project plan**, ticking off each stage.
notes.12: Knowledge is necessary and cheap to deliver, and almost never sufficient. The slide's test case is smoking: awareness of harm is near-universal, and change needed prices, bans, cues and norms. **If knowledge changed behaviour, no doctor would smoke.** Keep that sentence ready for any meeting where someone proposes more awareness.
notes.13: Name the gap before choosing the response: information closes the knowledge gap, benefit framing and emotion the attitude gap, visible social proof the norm gap, and cues, defaults and reduced friction the intention-action gap. **The last gap is the hardest and most neglected**, and communication is worst at it.
notes.14: Intentions leak. The chart is illustrative, but the lesson is real: between intention and action sit forgetting and friction, which are met by a timely reminder and removing a step. Asking someone to name when and where they will act raises follow-through. **Convert the intention that already exists.**
notes.15: Memorise five reasons intentions fail with their fixes: forgetting (a cue), friction (remove a step), habit (attach to a routine), present bias (immediate or visible benefit), competing demands (cut the time cost). **Attach the new act to an existing routine**, the most reliable and free fix: wash after the toilet.
notes.16: Many behaviours are watched and judged by family and neighbours: antenatal visits by the mother-in-law, vasectomy by male peers, menstrual hygiene by elders, toilet use by the hamlet. The person acting is often not the person deciding. **So the gatekeeper audience in Section 6 often matters more.**
notes.17: Structural barriers sit outside the individual: no toilet, an absent nurse, a four-hour walk, a lost day's wage. Diagnosing one as an attitude problem is the most expensive mistake in SBCC. **Find structural barriers in formative research**, since discovering them at evaluation is the standard failure.
notes.18: Ability beats motivation in the table: high ability with low motivation often succeeds, and low ability with high motivation still fails. So reduce friction first and then motivate. Programmes over-invest in the motivation column **because communication budgets can buy it**. Check where your own budget sits.
notes.19: Treat this as the course in five lines: find the real barrier, separate the gaps, address norms, flag structural blocks, make it easy. The right column shows the shortcut each step invites. A week of formative research costs less than a campaign aimed at the wrong barrier, **and it is the step most often cut**.
notes.21: A theory tells you what to ask about, and formative research tells you what is true here. Treat theories as diagnostic instruments and avoid using them as templates. Programmes that design straight from a theory address **whichever construct the theory emphasises**, skipping the diagnosis. The three classics follow.
notes.22: Learn the HBM constructs as six questions: could it happen to me, would it be serious, will acting help, what will it cost me, what prompts me now, can I do it. The slide's closing point: **barriers decide the outcome most often and are addressed least**, because they point at cost.
notes.23: Use the HBM to structure questions in place of statements. The table pairs each question with the statement it replaces: ask 'what would it cost you to go?' in place of 'please attend'. The last row, who decides whether she goes, **sits outside the HBM** and is often the operative answer in South Asia.
notes.24: TPB builds intention from three things: attitude, subjective norm and perceived control, with intention leading to behaviour. Ajzen's addition over Reasoned Action is perceived behavioural control. The model's value is separating three things campaigns merge. **Intention predicts behaviour only weakly**, so strong levers do not guarantee action.
notes.25: Match the message to the weak lever: attitude calls for a vivid benefit, norms for respected others doing it, control for demonstration and simplification. Formative research finds the weak lever. Without it, teams write the attitude message, **the one they find easiest**, and may preach when the block is felt control.
notes.26: People move through stages (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance) and do not change in one leap. The table gives a wrong message for each stage, such as a detailed how-to for someone not yet considering change and more facts for someone weighing pros and cons. The stages are contested, so **use them as a design heuristic**.
notes.27: Read across the three columns: stage, communication job, channel. Mass media suits precontemplation, peers and mid-media suit contemplation, interpersonal contact suits preparation and action, community and norms suit maintenance. **Interpersonal contact before anyone is contemplating is expensive and premature.** Segment by stage.
notes.28: No single theory explains everything. Take HBM for perceived barriers and benefits, TPB for norms and control, stages for readiness, social cognitive theory for self-efficacy and modelling, and COM-B as the checklist. **Say which construct your design targets.** COM-B comes later and collapses most of these.
notes.30: Individual theories explain the person, and the socio-ecological model reminds you of the layers around them: family and peers, community, institutions and services, policy and society. It works as a checklist and stops designs from touching only the inner layer. **The binding constraint is often in the outer layers.**
notes.31: Bandura's mechanism: people learn by watching others, especially similar others who are rewarded. So show the behaviour being done, show the reward and use models like the audience in age, caste, income and setting. This is the theory behind **role-model storytelling and entertainment-education**.
notes.32: Self-efficacy is belief in your ability to do a specific behaviour, and it is built by mastery, modelling and trusted encouragement. The slide ranks mastery first, which is why **demonstration beats explanation**. Because efficacy is behaviour-specific, a woman confident about immunisation may need separate work on negotiating a hospital delivery.
notes.33: Rogers described adoption in waves, starting with a small risk-tolerant group, then early adopters, then an early majority of about a third. The proportions are regularities and no law of nature. The insight is sequence: **measuring coverage against the whole population from month one makes the early phase look like failure**.
notes.34: Use Rogers for sequencing: reach innovators and early adopters first, rely on opinion leaders to bridge to the majority, give the early majority proof from people like them, and let norms move the late majority. Opinion leaders are **rarely the formally powerful**, so identify them locally in formative research.
notes.35: Descriptive norms say what people do, injunctive norms what they approve of. The classic backfire is saying 'too many still defecate in the open', which tells people it is normal. **Lead with the injunctive norm or a trend** ('more families every month') where the descriptive norm is against you.
notes.36: Where a behaviour is governed by norms, the first person to change bears a social cost, and collective change removes it. Public commitments, community declarations, visible markers and collective action all shift the shared expectation. The slide ties this to **CLTS-style triggering** in Section 10.
notes.38: Behavioural economics says people use shortcuts and are swayed by framing in ways that are systematic and predictable. The word that matters is predictable: these deviations can be designed for. It complements Sections 3 and 4 and **explains the intention-action gap** those models leave open.
notes.39: COM-B says a behaviour needs capability, opportunity and motivation at once, and removing any one makes it fail. That is why it works as a diagnostic: find the missing component and the type of intervention follows. It sits at the centre of **Michie's Behaviour Change Wheel**.
notes.40: Use the three diagnostic questions in order: do they know how and feel able, does the context allow it, do they want to in the moment. The remedies run from teaching to fixing access to framing and incentives. In development settings **opportunity is the missing component most often** and communication addresses it least.
notes.41: Five biases, five design responses: bring the benefit forward for present bias, frame as avoiding a loss, change the default, show what similar others do, make the case vivid. Effects are small but reliable, and **a default change costs nothing and applies to everyone**. Treat biases as levers.
notes.42: A nudge steers behaviour predictably without forbidding options or changing incentives. The five examples are default, framing, commitment, reminder and simplification. The slide calls simplification the least glamorous and most effective: **cutting a four-step process to two changes uptake more than most messaging**. A large payment is not a nudge.
notes.43: The environment is never neutral: the default, the order of options, the friction and what is salient all steer choice. Someone designed them, or nobody did. Walk through your own service as a user and **count the frictions**, which the slide calls the cheapest diagnostic in the course.
notes.44: EAST gives four checks: easy, attractive, social, timely. It is deliberately crude so a non-specialist can apply it. Timeliness is the most under-used: a reminder the morning of beats one the week before, and both cost the same. **Test every intervention against all four letters.**
notes.45: Nudges work at the margin: they close an intention-action gap, raise uptake cheaply and work quietly. They cannot supply a missing service or overcome a structural barrier. A nudge to wash hands is no answer to a village with no water. **Apply the transparency test**: could you tell the audience exactly what you did?
notes.47: 'The community' is five audiences in one village: a new mother, her mother-in-law, the ASHA, the village head and the absent husband. Each sees the behaviour differently. Choose the audience whose change is the binding constraint. In much of South Asia **that is the gatekeeper**, and the person performing the behaviour may matter less.
notes.48: Segment by barrier, because two women of the same age and income can face different obstacles. Demographic segmentation is easy and tells you who they are, and it never tells you why they are not acting. Add role (doer or gatekeeper) where permission is the constraint, and stage where the audience is mixed.
notes.49: Use three layers: primary (the person whose behaviour must change), secondary (those close who shape it) and influencing (leaders and policy). Budgets usually go all to the primary audience while the decision often sits with the secondary one. **Design at least one message and channel for the secondary audience.**
notes.50: Gatekeepers are often treated as obstacles. The table treats them as an audience with their own motivators: status and a healthy grandchild for the mother-in-law, cost and time for the husband, being consulted for the elder, workload and recognition for the frontline worker. **A campaign that bypasses the mother-in-law invites her to block it.**
notes.51: Pair every barrier with a motivator that can outweigh it, and find both lists in research. The table makes one exception: lost wages is the barrier motivators rarely outweigh, so the answer there is compensation or timing. **Motivators are rarely 'health' in the abstract**: people act for love, pride, money and belonging.
notes.52: A persona turns a segment into a named person with a routine, one barrier and one motivator, so the team argues about one concrete human. Sunita's example names who decides (her mother-in-law) and how to reach her (the ASHA and her husband). **Build personas from real interviews**, since workshop inventions encode assumptions.
notes.53: The goal is one sharp insight in the person's own emotional logic. Compare the pairs: 'mothers lack awareness' against 'she has heard it and does not believe it applies to her'. The test: **does the insight suggest a message you would not have written otherwise?** If it does not, it restates the problem.
notes.55: Formative research is the listening done before any message. The table maps five questions to the decisions they inform: the assumed gap, the theory, the message, the messenger and the copy. It need not be large: twenty in-depth interviews and two days of observation answer most for one behaviour in one district. **It is skipped because it sits between funding and output.**
notes.56: Each question decides a design element: who already does it (your models), the real barrier (the message), who they trust (the messenger), their words (the copy), their channels (the mix). The slide stresses that none can be answered from a desk. **Copy written in programme vocabulary is discounted as official.**
notes.57: Pick methods by purpose: interviews for sensitive behaviour, focus groups for norms and language, observation for what people do, free listing for local categories, quick surveys for how common. Observation most often contradicts the others, which is the say-do gap. **Use focus groups for the audience's words** and leave prevalence to a survey.
notes.58: Learn the five steps in order: one specific behaviour, interview doers and non-doers, compare beliefs, rank the differences, design against the top ones. The discipline is finding which plausible barriers actually separate the groups. **'Good hygiene' cannot be analysed; 'washing hands with soap after cleaning a child' can.**
notes.59: Doers are your assets and non-doers show the barrier, and the biggest gap between them is where to aim first. The doer and non-doer comparison is the nearest thing formative research has to a control group. **Doers are also your best models and messengers**, as they have changed in the same setting.
notes.60: Probe the constructs and the last actual episode instead of general practice. The better questions ask what she gave last time and why, who decides whether the child goes, and to be shown where she washes hands. **Knowledge questions produce the answer the respondent thinks is expected**, so reported knowledge is high and predicts little.
notes.61: Qualitative work finds the why, the mechanism, the language and the barrier, and a quick quantitative scan finds how many and where. Use existing data first (NFHS, HMIS, district reports), since much sizing is done and free. **Do the qualitative work first**, or the survey will ask the wrong questions in the wrong words.
notes.62: Formative research continues into pretesting and monitoring as a habit of checking assumptions. The slide's budget warning is the takeaway: programmes with no time for research spend far more later fixing campaigns that did not land. **Put research in the budget as its own line.**
notes.64: Write the SOCO before any creative work: one audience, one behaviour, one change, one reason. The test is length: if it takes more than one sentence, the campaign is trying to do more than one thing. **Disagreements about what the communication is for should surface here**, before any creative work is made.
notes.65: The table shows the arithmetic of memory: one behaviour on a poster is remembered, three perhaps one, five none, and a logo with five behaviours leaves the logo. Pressure to combine comes from budget efficiency and every department wanting space. **One behaviour, one audience, one ask per piece**, with sequenced pieces for the rest.
notes.66: Use emotion to open and reason to close, with the action stated plainly at the end. Rational appeals give credibility and what to do, emotional appeals give memorability and why it matters to me. **A purely emotional appeal leaves people moved and unsure; a purely rational one is understood and forgotten.**
notes.67: Fear works when paired with a doable action, a personal threat, high self-efficacy and sparing use. It fails when the action is unclear, the threat feels remote, people feel helpless or it is the whole campaign. The failure is denial and avoidance. **Never present a threat without an immediately available action.**
notes.68: Test a message on five qualities: simple (repeatable after one hearing), concrete (a named action), credible, emotional, story-shaped. These are five of the Heath brothers' six criteria; the sixth is Unexpected. **Concrete is where development communication fails most**: 'wash with soap after the toilet' is an action, 'improve hygiene' is a value.
notes.69: Source credibility is part of the message. A relatable neighbour suits everyday behaviours, a frontline worker answers doubts, an elder shifts norms and permission, a celebrity gives attention and reach, an official gives legitimacy. The first row is under-used and the fourth over-used. **For a behaviour needing permission, the elder is necessary.**
notes.70: Pretest comprehension, attractiveness, acceptability, persuasion and self-reference ('that is not about people like me'). Eight to twelve members of the real audience catch most serious problems in a day. The commonest finding is a misread image or metaphor, the **curse of knowledge in visual form**. One afternoon saves crores in wasted print runs.
notes.71: A call to action needs what, where and when. The table's right column shows each: the 9-month measles shot, soap before feeding, the sub-centre on Tuesday morning, the toilet at the end of your lane. Adding where and when is free and **the commonest omission in otherwise well-made material**.
notes.73: Mass media reaches millions and persuades shallowly, while interpersonal contact reaches few and changes behaviour more. The trade-off is structural, so a single-channel budget is a choice about which half to lose. The chart is illustrative. **Cost per person moves the opposite way**, which is the planning problem.
notes.74: Learn the four channel families with one strength and one weakness each: mass media (reach and norms; weak persuasion), mid-media and folk (local credibility; weak scale), interpersonal (persuasion; reach and cost), digital (timeliness; reaching those without phones). The last weakness is **gendered in South Asia**, since phone use is lower among women.
notes.75: Use mass media for awareness and for signalling that a behaviour is becoming the new normal, including to the less literate. It cannot answer a family's particular doubt or demonstrate a skill. Radio is substantial in rural South Asia and is often underestimated. **Budget separately for the interpersonal contact that converts.**
notes.76: Mid-media includes nukkad natak, puppets, folk song, video vans and wall paintings. Each has a particular strength, such as humour for taboo topics, travelling songs and standing cues. The trade-off is consistency: a live performance varies by troupe and night, so **monitor message fidelity** and avoid assuming it.
notes.77: Interpersonal communication allows questions, tailoring, demonstration and trust, which is where intention most often becomes action. It is the most expensive channel per person and depends on the worker's time. **Adding an IPC component adds to someone's day**, and that person is usually already full.
notes.78: Community mobilisation organises women's collectives, SHGs and village health and sanitation committees so people hold the behaviour as a shared commitment. Collective action changes the norm and gives social cover. Where an SHG network exists, it is **usually the cheapest platform and the one with most existing trust**.
notes.79: Digital channels are cheap, targeted and two-way, and the reminder is the highest-value use because it hits the intention-action gap at the moment of decision. Phone access skews male, richer, younger and urban. **Check whose phone it is**: a message about a woman's health to a household number may reach her husband.
notes.80: Choose channels by audience, job, stage and moment. Layer them so they repeat one consistent message, since three different messages compete. Sequence deliberately: mass media first to make the behaviour thinkable, interpersonal contact after, reminders at the decision point. **Budget realistically**, as IPC is powerful and costly to scale.
notes.82: The campaign cycle is a loop: analyse, design, develop and pretest, implement, monitor and evaluate, then back into analysis. The table shows what feeds back at each stage. **Build a mid-course review with explicit licence to change the creative**, or monitoring produces a report and no change.
notes.83: Write the strategy first: behaviour, audiences and barriers, SOCO, channels and messengers, indicators. Logo and tagline come last. A strategy is also what lets you say no to the fifth message someone wants added. **A slogan with no strategy behind it is clever, memorable and about nothing specific.**
notes.84: People support what they help create. When a community diagnoses its own problem, the change holds, and outside messengers can catalyse a decision but cannot make it. The table contrasts compliance while watched with change that holds. **Ask what happens at exit**: an externally owned behaviour ends with the programme.
notes.85: CLTS drops subsidies and lecturing: facilitators help a community confront open defecation and decide together, with local solutions and an ODF goal. Its mechanism is norm change, so nobody bears the cost of being first. Note the critique: **triggering can shame the poorest households**, who often lack the means to build.
notes.86: Entertainment-education works through Bandura: viewers model relatable, rewarded characters. The effect depends on the story being good enough to watch for its own sake, because audiences watch voluntarily. **A drama written mainly to carry messages is usually a poor drama**, and a poor drama models nothing.
notes.87: ASHAs, ANMs and anganwadi workers are the backbone of interpersonal SBCC: last-mile, local idiom, familiar face, repeat contact. They cost time already committed, training and supervision. **Any new communication task routed through ASHAs should say what it displaces**, because their day is already full and largely incentive-based.
notes.88: Participatory groups let members discuss problems, plan and support each other, so peer support sustains change, a shared norm lowers the cost of being first and collective analysis surfaces local barriers. The slide says these approaches have among the strongest evidence for maternal and newborn health in South Asia. **A lecture to a group is a different intervention.**
notes.89: Sustaining change takes five moves: repeat and reinforce, build local ownership, make the behaviour visible, remove friction, celebrate progress. The slide says the most durable is removing friction, since motivation decays and ease does not. **Budget the maintenance phase**, because funding usually stops when reinforcement matters most.
notes.91: Walk the chain from outputs to reach, exposure, knowledge and attitude, behaviour and impact. Outputs prove you spent the money, reach that people could have seen it, exposure that they did, knowledge that it landed, behaviour that it worked. **Where behaviour did not move but knowledge did, you have located the failure.**
notes.92: Pick one indicator per level: recall, ORS knowledge, neighbours' approval, intention to immunise, children fully immunised. The norm indicator is the one most often omitted and the most diagnostic in norm-governed behaviours, and it is a single survey question. **Verify behaviour against records** where possible, since self-report overstates handwashing.
notes.93: Handwashing shows the course in one behaviour: from telling people germs exist to a habit tied to specific moments (after the toilet, before feeding a child), with cues, disgust, nurture and repetition. The chart is illustrative and shows no actual programme figures. **Handwashing at a named moment can become automatic; handwashing in general cannot.**
notes.94: Mission Indradhanush paired service delivery drives with ASHA mobilisation, local influencers and rumour response. The slide's lesson is that communication and service must move together. The rumour response matters most, since hesitancy often follows a **specific circulating claim** that generic messaging misses.
notes.95: Swachh Bharat combined infrastructure, mass media and celebrity, CLTS-style triggering and ODF declarations, and the right column lists what is contested for each. The lasting lesson is the gap between construction and use: **a toilet built is an output, and a toilet used is the behaviour**.
notes.96: ORS is a success because it was one simple behaviour, low cost and home-based, promoted consistently through several channels over decades. The slide wants you to cite it against the pressure for novelty. **Changing the campaign every two years is a common way to lose accumulated recall.**
notes.97: Five ethical rules: avoid stigma, be truthful, respect autonomy, do no harm, be inclusive. The table adds transparency. The fourth row is serious: a message urging a woman to act against her household's wishes can leave her bearing the consequences alone. **Ask what happens to the person after they act on it, at home.**
notes.98: Four traps: stigma (shaming those who lack means), norm ('most people still don't'), fear (threat without a doable action) and blame (making individuals responsible for a structural gap). One drafting question catches all: **who could this message hurt, and can they do what it asks?** The norm trap is easy to commit by reporting a low prevalence.
notes.99: Use the reading list by purpose: Rogers for how practices spread, Cialdini for norms, Thaler and Sunstein and EAST for nudges, Michie for COM-B, Johns Hopkins CCP for practice guidance. Start with the Behaviour Change Wheel for programme design. **Read one theory source and one worked campaign evaluation together.**
